output.brief: The evidence points mainly at the revised merit scholarship schedule, not the Admissions Office. Yield fell sharply only in the tiers whose awards were cut: Dean's went from 45.2% to 31.9% and Merit from 44.9% to 32.3%. Yield stayed flat in Presidential (awards unchanged) and no-award groups. The applicant pool was larger and slightly stronger, so a weaker pool does not explain it. Early-action students got decisions on time under the old system, yet their yield fell as much as regular decision (45.2% to 37.8% versus 39.0% to 31.5%). Slow regular-decision turnaround is therefore not the main driver, though it was real and may have cost individual students. I did not check whether the portal lost documents, so that stays open. I'm fairly confident (about 80%) but this is not a controlled test. One gap: the tier data doesn't split early action from regular decision. Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee with restored awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers and the net-revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Separately, set a regular-decision turnaround target with monthly reporting. Hold the vendor rebuild until the document-loss question is checked.
